At the beginning of The Office, Dunder Mifflin is presented as an underperforming paper business in a digital world. Sales are down, and staff is mostly uninspired, filling their days with pranks and nonsense. At one point, corporate talks about closing Scranton branch. Then something happens: sales start going up, huge clients are landed, and Scranton inexplicably becomes the most profitable branch in the whole company.

My theory is that the camera crew unintentionally caused this to happen, simply by being there.

We know that Michael Scott doesn't mind putting on a show for the cameras, as evident in the first episode where he calls Jim into his office and delivers the infamous "grasshopper" speech. But we also know that he's bumbling and unaware even when cameras aren't around, like in Scott's Tots.

He also hates being disliked, and will go to great lengths to avoid uncomfortable conversations.

I suspect that, before the cameras, Michael didn't call nearly as many meetings, or host nearly as many useless events and fundraisers. This erratic, unpredictable behavior is the result of him slipping into his "Michael Scott, world's best boss" character. He might not even realize he's doing it, but he is.

It's in his nature to want to steal the spotlight, but before there was a spotlight, he wanted to be liked in other ways. That's why Jim, Pam, Kevin, and their coworkers get away with so much. He never told them to "get back to work". He avoided those conversations.

In a later episode, Phyllis says "we find little times throughout the day" in response to a question asking how they manage to get any work done. But it hasn't always been this way. When Scranton was on the verge of collapse, no one thought much about wasting time, but now that Michael is constantly interrupting them, the pressure is on. They have to find "little times" to work, and are working more than ever before.

And it's all thanks to the camera crew causing Michael Scott to act like an even more extreme version of Michael Scott.
